analysis.one_liner: Makes it a federal crime for custody officers to withhold medical care from people in distress.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on June 18, 2020 and died there without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require federal law enforcement officers and prison officials to get immediate medical help for anyone in federal custody who shows medical distress, including trouble breathing. An officer who negligently fails to do so, and the person suffers pain, injury, or death as a result, could be fined or jailed for up to a year. It would also require Inspector General investigations of every such incident, a confidential complaint process, and training for officers. It is named for Andrew Kearse, who died in 2017 after a medical emergency during an arrest.
analysis.who_benefits: People in federal custody — federal prisoners, people held in federal jails, and anyone arrested by a federal officer — who would gain a legal guarantee of immediate medical attention, an independent investigation when it is denied, and a way to file confidential complaints. Their families would gain a federal crime to point to when a loved one dies asking for help.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a new federal crime: a federal officer or prison official who negligently fails to get immediate medical attention for a person in custody showing medical distress, causing unnecessary pain, injury, or death, can be fined or imprisoned for up to one year.

Requires the agency Inspector General to investigate every instance where medical attention is denied and the person is harmed or dies, and to refer negligent cases to the Attorney General for prosecution.
Establishes a confidential complaint process so officers' failures can be reported, and requires training so all covered officials know how to get medical help.
Includes breathing difficulties in the definition of medical distress, the condition at issue in the case the bill is named for.

analysis.who_pays: Federal law enforcement officers and Bureau of Prisons personnel, who would face personal criminal liability — a fine, up to one year in prison, or both — for negligently denying medical care, plus mandatory investigations and training at their agencies.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal law enforcement and prison officers

drawbacks.text: The maximum penalty is modest — a fine or up to one year in prison — and enforcement depends entirely on Inspector Generals investigating and the Justice Department choosing to prosecute its own or partner officers, so accountability would rely heavily on the willingness of the government to charge its own personnel.

The negligence standard applies to officers facing fast-moving emergencies, and critics of custody liability laws argue this can pressure officers toward calling for transport in every borderline case and create a chilling effect on judgment calls.
The bill covers only federal custody; it would do nothing about the state and local policing contexts where most such deaths occur.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a concrete federal guarantee that people in government custody get medical help when they show distress, backed by real penalties and independent investigations; the cost falls almost entirely on federal officers and their agencies in added liability and training. The main weaknesses are the light maximum penalty and the fact that prosecution depends on the Justice Department's own discretion. It is a narrow bill — federal custody only — but the mechanism is straightforward and the cost to the public is minimal.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never held a hearing or voted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on June 18, 2020, joined by five cosponsors — Senators Gillibrand, Markey, Blumenthal, Sanders, and Hirono.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary.
No further action was ever taken: no committee hearing, no markup, no floor vote appears in the record for the rest of the 116th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal law enforcement officers and prison officials who would have faced the new criminal liability are better off, because the bill never advanced. Agencies avoid the mandatory investigations, complaint process, and training the bill would have required.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal law enforcement and prison officers

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so opposition was never recorded; all six sponsors were Democrats or an Independent, and the bill died in the Republican-led Judiciary Committee without action.

industries.industry: Federal law enforcement and corrections officers
industries.note: The bill would expose federal officers and Bureau of Prisons staff to personal criminal liability, fines, and up to a year in prison for negligently denying medical care, plus mandatory Inspector General investigations. Their interest in avoiding liability runs against a legal right to medical attention for the people they hold.

industries.industry: Federal law enforcement agencies and the Bureau of Prisons
industries.note: Agencies would bear new training obligations, complaint processes, and investigations of their personnel, but the bill also gives them a clear standard to follow and could reduce liability from civil suits over deaths in custody.
